clue.text: High point when 12 leaving party hit rum

indicators.note: leaving says the party word departs from the number word, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: twelve is a dozen
DO is a common word for a party or celebration

indicators.note: rum in its sense of strange or odd tells us the next word's letters come out oddly arranged

explanation.surface: Someone recalls their best moment, when a dozen guests left a party and a rum punch did its work.
explanation.walkthrough: The 12 looks like a cross-reference to another clue but is simply the number twelve. 'leaving' removes DO from DOZEN to leave ZEN; 'rum' rearranges HIT as ITH.
explanation.definitionFit: A zenith is the peak or highest point of something, literally the point of the sky directly overhead.

clue.text: Minor difference in identical situation, finally

indicators.note: a difference made in the word identical means its letters are altered into a new order
finally points to the closing letter of the word situation

explanation.surface: Someone spots a small discrepancy in a supposedly matching situation at the last moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' gives N, the last letter of 'situation'; 'difference in' then shuffles IDENTICAL plus N.
explanation.definitionFit: Something incidental is minor or secondary, occurring only as a side issue.

clue.text: Accomplishes chore with wicket — cricket series over

parts.note: W is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for wicket
the Ashes is the Test cricket series between England and Australia
up can mean over or finished, as in time is up

explanation.surface: A cricket report: a wicket falls, and the Ashes series is over.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ashes is the long-running Test cricket series played between England and Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Washing up is the chore of cleaning the dishes, so someone who washes up has done that household task.

clue.text: Possible border patrol's leader, one getting hammered

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter, here taken from patrol's

parts.note: a rivet is a metal pin that is hammered flat to fasten things

explanation.surface: A border patrol's chief ends up getting drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one getting hammered' looks like a drunk but is a rivet, struck with a hammer. 'Possible' marks the definition as an example: privet is one plant used to make a border.
explanation.definitionFit: Privet is a shrub widely planted as a hedge, so it is one possible garden border.

clue.text: Fair fool turns up with fur

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means the word reads from bottom to top, so it is reversed

parts.note: a sap is a gullible fool
sable is a prized fur from a small mammal

explanation.surface: A foolish person shows up in a fur coat, and is judged to look fair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns up' reverses SAP to PAS, which sits on top of SABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Passable means fair or adequate, good enough without being excellent.

clue.text: Violate the law when refining crude

indicators.note: crude, like crude oil before processing, tells us the word refining is in a raw, rearranged state

explanation.surface: An oil company breaks the rules while processing crude oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crude' rearranges the letters of REFINING.
explanation.definitionFit: To infringe is to break or violate a rule, law or right.

clue.text: Tunnel regularly shocking, off limits

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of the word Tunnel

parts.note: awful and shocking are synonyms for something dreadful

explanation.surface: A tunnel that is often in terrible condition is closed to the public.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of Tunnel: U, N, L.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unlawful is forbidden by law, so it is off limits.

clue.text: Complaint over crossed lines brings change

parts.note: a complaint can be an illness, such as flu
two crossed lines form the letter X

explanation.surface: A grumble about crossed telephone lines leads to some change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' reads as a grumble but means an illness. In a down clue 'over' places FLU above X.
explanation.definitionFit: Flux is a state of continual change, as in a situation in flux.

clue.text: Northerner's gods have one, it's said

definitions.note: the definition is Northerner, with the 's standing for is

indicators.note: it's said tells us the word is spoken, so we want a word that sounds the same

parts.note: the idiom 'in the lap of the gods' gives the gods a lap

explanation.surface: Someone from the far north explains their gods each have something, according to legend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the lap of the gods' means beyond human control; so the gods have a lap, which sounds like LAPP.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lapp is one of the Sami people of far northern Scandinavia, so a northerner.

clue.text: Underside of structure pliable, provided held back

indicators.note: held means the first word keeps the second within it

parts.note: pliable and soft both describe something easily bent

indicators.note: back means the word for provided is read in reverse

parts.note: if means provided, as in provided that

explanation.surface: An engineer says a structure's underside is flexible, provided it is held back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns IF into FI, and 'held' places it inside SOFT.
explanation.definitionFit: A soffit is the underside of an architectural element such as an arch, eave or balcony.

clue.text: Start off first in event

indicators.note: first tells us the word for off comes before the word for start in the answer

parts.note: food that has gone off is high
a start is a sudden jump of surprise

explanation.surface: An athlete is told when the event begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start off' looks like the beginning of a race, but 'Start' gives JUMP and 'off' gives HIGH, which 'first' puts in front.
explanation.definitionFit: The high jump is an athletics event in which competitors leap over a raised bar.

clue.text: Actually live

definitions.meaning: used to mean in fact, as it turns out
broadcast in real time, while events are taking place

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both 'in fact' and 'at the very moment of occurrence', as with a live broadcast.

clue.text: He's solemnly dressed, though sounds like I have less on?

indicators.note: sounds like tells us to say a phrase and hear another word

parts.note: I is the setter, Paul, and having less on makes one barer

explanation.surface: A soberly dressed man jokes that he is barer than usual.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter of this puzzle is Paul, so 'I' is PAUL; 'I have less on' becomes 'Paul barer', said like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pallbearer carries a coffin at a funeral and is dressed in sober mourning clothes.

clue.text: Top mark only received

indicators.note: received means the first word takes the second inside it

parts.note: a pock is a mark on the skin, as in pockmark
lone means sole or only

explanation.surface: A pupil gets the best grade and nothing else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top mark' looks like an A grade, but 'Top' is the definition (a garment) and 'mark' gives POCK, which 'received' wraps around LONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A polo neck is a sweater or top with a high, close, turned-over collar.

clue.text: Extreme characters in cooler maintaining bitter and twisted schedule

indicators.note: maintaining means the outer pair holds the following letters inside it
the extreme characters of cooler are its first and last letters

parts.note: bitter is a type of British beer, an ale

indicators.note: twisted means the letters of the word and are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone bitter and twisted keeps a timetable in the fridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extreme characters in' gives C and R from cooler; 'twisted' turns AND into NDA; 'maintaining' puts ALE plus NDA between them. Bitter is a kind of British beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A calendar is a schedule of dates and events, such as a fixtures calendar.

clue.text: Stage attraction a joke

parts.note: a leg is a stage of a journey or competition
pull is attraction, as in the pull of the sea

explanation.surface: A theatre draw turns out to be just a gag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stage' suggests the theatre but means a leg of a journey.
explanation.definitionFit: A leg-pull is a practical joke or a hoax, from the idiom of pulling someone's leg.

clue.text: Prestigious clue for "tram"

parts.note: the pieces read as an instruction: a word for market, mart, going up in a down entry spells the clue's word tram

explanation.surface: A setter proudly offers a clue for the word tram.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer split as UP MARKET is itself a clue, with MART (market) going up to give TRAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Upmarket means aimed at wealthy customers, so expensive and prestigious.

clue.text: Olympic officials, having tucked into Spanish food, almost finished pudding

indicators.note: tucked into means the officials go inside the food word
almost finished means the last letter of the food word is dropped

parts.note: tapas are small Spanish dishes
the IOC is the International Olympic Committee

explanation.surface: Olympic officials, having eaten tapas, have nearly finished their dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost finished' cuts TAPAS to TAPA, and 'having tucked into' places IOC inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tapioca is a starchy pudding made from cassava pearls cooked in milk.

clue.text: Source of misery accompanied by ring — bitterness follows, very acidic?

definitions.text: Source of misery accompanied by ring — bitterness follows, very acidic?

indicators.note: the source of a word is its opening letter, here from misery

parts.note: a ring is round, shaped like the letter O
bile means bitterness or bad temper
a very acidic liquid has a pH of one

explanation.surface: A gloomy account of something that rings and leaves a bitter, sour taste.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue describes the device: a source of misery that comes with a ring. On pH scales, one is extremely acidic, so PH ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A mobile phone rings at inconvenient moments, making it a well-known source of irritation and misery.

clue.text: Repressed writer, one bleating

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument
a tup is a ram, a sheep that bleats

explanation.surface: An author feels stifled and keeps complaining like a sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: TUP is a British word for a ram.
explanation.definitionFit: Pent-up feelings are held in and repressed rather than expressed.

clue.text: One writing nonsense disheartens composer

indicators.note: disheartens means the heart, or central letter, of the composer's name is removed

parts.note: Franz Lehar was the Hungarian composer of The Merry Widow

explanation.surface: A writer of rubbish dismays a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disheartens' removes the middle letter H from LEHAR. Edward Lear wrote nonsense verse such as The Owl and the Pussy-cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear was a Victorian writer famous for nonsense poems and limericks.

clue.text: Stone round and white, virtually

parts.note: a round shape is like the letter O

indicators.note: virtually means almost all of the word, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: pale means white or lacking colour

explanation.surface: A stone described as round and nearly white.
explanation.walkthrough: 'virtually' trims PALE to PAL.
explanation.definitionFit: An opal is a gemstone known for its milky, iridescent colours.

clue.text: Celebrity making a comeback, grabbing bed with body that's heavenly

indicators.note: grabbing means the reversed word holds the next piece within it
making a comeback means the word for celebrity is turned backwards

parts.note: a name is a celebrity, as in a big name
a funeral pyre is a bed of wood with a body laid on it

explanation.surface: A star returns to the stage, grabbing a bed for a body that is out of this world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making a comeback' turns NAME into EMAN; 'grabbing' puts PYRE inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Empyrean means of the highest heaven, so celestial or heavenly.

clue.text: Mean people producing games without limits

indicators.note: without limits means losing the first and last letters

parts.note: Nintendo is the Japanese company that makes video games

explanation.surface: Stingy people make games with no rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without limits' strips N and O from the ends of NINTENDO.
explanation.definitionFit: To mean something is to intend it, as in I meant to call.

clue.text: Evil snakes in the grass no longer worried

indicators.note: in means the rearranged letters sit within the grass word

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass growing by water

indicators.note: snakes as a verb means winds about, so the letters of Evil are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is relieved now the wicked snakes in the grass are gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'snakes' looks like a noun, but it is a verb signalling the anagram of EVIL into LIEV, placed 'in' REED.
explanation.definitionFit: To be relieved is to be freed from anxiety, no longer worried.

clue.text: Christian appearing fearful?

parts.note: a member of the Society of Friends, read playfully as someone who trembles with fear

explanation.definitionFit: Quakers are members of a Christian denomination, and the name literally suggests one who trembles.
